newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - April 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH

-- TORIES POST REPACKAGED MAIL SELL-OFF The Conservative Party yesterday made a manifesto commitment to consider new options in privatisation of the Post Office. Plans to sell off Parcelforce have been revived, as well as plans to privatise London Underground, with profits being used to upgrade the network. Labour attacked the Post Office plans, but is expected to reveal greater commitment to commercial freedom for the postal service in its own manifesto today.

-- FIRED PYKETT READY TO SUE COWIE GROUP Former Cowie Financial Holdings managing director Neil Pykett, recently dismissed on gross misconduct allegations, will sue parent company Cowie Group for unfair dismissal if shareholders vote him out next Wednesday. Mr Pykett had earlier given three years' notice of his resignation, and claims his dismissal stems from his intention to inform the Stock Market of his decision. He has the backing of former Cowie Group chairman and largest individual shareholder Sir Tom Cowie for the meeting.

-- PROFITS TOP 1 BILLION POUNDS AGAIN AT LLOYD'S Lloyd's of London has announced a pre-tax profit of just over 1 billion pounds stg for 1994, only slightly down on the previous year. The figure is just below the forecast level after the strength of sterling undermined profits. A further decline is expected
for the 1995 underwriting year. THE TIMES

-- CITY FEARS EFFECTS OF BOOM IN CREDIT Consumer credit rose by a record 1.22 billion pounds stg in February, increasing fears in the City that the economy was booming out of control. This compares with the 884 million pound rise in January and is well above expectations of a rise in the region of 1 billion pounds. Analysts said the figure would increase pressure for a rates rise after the election.
-- GEC TAKES ON ALCATEL IN BID BATTLE FOR THOMSON GEC

despite being in partnership with French group Alcatel-Alsthorm, has independently entered the bidding race for French defence company Thomson-CSF. A 58 per cent stake in Thomson is being sold by the French government, and GEC is in direct competition for it with Alcatel and British Aerospace partner Lagardere Groupe.

-- CELLNET COUNTS THE COST OF CUT-OFFS Cellnet last night released figures showing that it had recruited only 12,000 customers in the first quarter, well behind its rivals. The company attributed the figures to large-scale disconnection of non-paying customers and its decision to allow customers to cancel service with one month's notice instead of three. THE
GUARDIAN

-- CO-OP PROFITS AID DEFENCE The Co-operative Bank yesterday reported record profits for the third year running, providing further defence against Lancia Trust's takeover plans. Pre-tax profits rose 24 per cent to 45 million pounds stg, which the bank said was due to its ethical business and investment
approach.

-- BM SWITCHES TO AIRBUS Airbus Industrie yesterday won an order for 20 new aircraft from British Midland, a deal worth 625 million pounds stg. British Midland will take delivery of 20 A320 planes over five years with an option allowing upgrading to the larger A321.

-- WOOLWICH FACES WINDFALL CHALLENGE Woolwich Building Society faces a legal challenge from one of its members to its exclusion of 35,000 savers from windfall bonuses created by its flotation. Mr Tony Webster, a 59-year-old guest house proprietor, will challenge the legality of the company's decision to impose a retrospective qualifying date when the case is heard by the Building Societies Commission on April 16. The flotation is scheduled for July 7. THE INDEPENDENT
-- SAUDI PRINCE TAKES FIVE PER CENT STAKE IN AILING APPLE

Prince al-Waleed bin Talal of Saudi Arabia yesterday revealed that he had bought 5 per cent of Apple for 115 million dollars US. Apple has been hit hard in recent times by Microsoft. The Prince's move follows his acquisition two weeks ago of a 5 per cent stake in troubled Trans World Airlines, and last week's revelation by Oracle Software Ralph Ellison that he was considering forming a coalition to bid for Apple.
-- MMC CALLS IN WATCHDOG OVER INVESTIGATION INTO BRITISH GAS

Gas watchdog Ofgas has been summoned back to a hearing by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission investigation pipeline charges by British Gas GAS.L. The move suggests the conclusion of the investigation will not be revealed until after the election, and that Ofgas has failed to win MMC support for its plans to slash British Gas's pipeline charges.

-- INVESTMENT AT UNIPART 'CUT IF LABOUR WINS' Unipart chief executive John Neill yesterday said he was considering halting investment plans if a Labour government implemented its trade union recognition policy. He said the policy was part of a plan to implement the European Social Chapter and claimed that Tony Blair's vision of a stakeholder economy was copied from one of his own speeches.
